questions.q: Why is converting a NumPy array to `std::vector<double>` a poor choice for a performance-sensitive binding?
options: std::vector cannot hold floating-point numbers
pybind11 does not support std::vector conversions at all
The conversion copies every element into the vector on the way in, and copies the result back out on the way back
NumPy arrays cannot be iterated over in C++ under any method
questions.explain: pybind11's STL conversion support copies data both directions. For large arrays that doubles the memory traffic compared to operating on the array's existing buffer directly.

questions.q: What does calling `.request()` on a `py::array_t<double>` return?
options: A new Python list containing copies of the array's elements
A `py::buffer_info` object exposing the array's raw pointer, shape, ndim, and strides
A boolean indicating whether the array is writable
A string describing the array's dtype
questions.explain: `.request()` returns a `py::buffer_info`, pybind11's description of the underlying memory — `.ptr`, `.shape`, `.ndim`, and `.strides` — without copying any data.

questions.q: In the `vectorizedPayoff` function, why is a brand-new `py::array_t<double>` allocated for the result instead of writing the payoffs back into the input array?
options: pybind11 requires every function to allocate at least one array
Writing into the caller's input array would silently mutate data the Python caller still expects to be unchanged
It is impossible to write into an existing array's buffer from C++
NumPy arrays are always read-only once passed into a compiled function
questions.explain: Mutating the caller's input array as a side effect of computing an output is surprising and error-prone; allocating a separate output array keeps the function's behavior predictable, matching what a normal NumPy function would do.

questions.q: Which header must be included to use `py::array_t` and the NumPy buffer-protocol support in pybind11?
options: <pybind11/pybind11.h> alone is sufficient
<pybind11/numpy.h>
<numpy/arrayobject.h> only, with no pybind11 header
<pybind11/stl.h>
questions.explain: `py::array_t` and the buffer-protocol helpers live in `<pybind11/numpy.h>`, which must be included in addition to the core `<pybind11/pybind11.h>` header.

questions.q: A binding indexes into `buf.ptr` without first checking `buf.ndim`. What real risk does skipping that check introduce?
options: None — pybind11 guarantees every array passed in is always one-dimensional
The function may silently misinterpret a 2-D or higher-dimensional array's memory as a flat 1-D buffer, reading or writing the wrong elements
The Python interpreter will refuse to start
NumPy will automatically reshape the array to match the function's expectations
questions.explain: A `py::array_t<double>` can be passed with any number of dimensions unless constrained; treating multi-dimensional data as flat 1-D without checking `ndim` and `shape` leads to logically wrong results rather than a clear error.
